claims.text: A blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK and CloudFormation produce an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
The SST team expanded beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure and found CDK/CloudFormation's AWS-centric nature a limitation.
AWS CDK supports AWS only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK language support is limited to TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi is faster due to direct execution.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi extensibility includes custom providers and workflows, while AWS CDK is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.
The linked Pulumi Insights product page describes improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired customization.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
The Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation page exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ and covers advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand workshop 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, and once Ion is stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST Ion deploys constructs (components) using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST stores its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has said, repeatedly since the rewrite shipped, that SST is architected on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST supports deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
Ion (SST v3 architecture) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs "What is SST" say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" says: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
Independent developers who compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture of SST built on the Pulumi engine.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, and a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.

The SST repository is now at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and its `platform/package.json` lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
In SST's deployment chain, the Pulumi engine diffs desired versus actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
`sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and those components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge) translate each resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs for SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine can run without a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside teams' own tools.
The same provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Cross-reference: the post links to /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, and /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/.
Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, states in its docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write any Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly as Pulumi resources within an SST app and deployed as part of the same app, because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub star count than SST itself.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode, and SST's release cadence is unchanged.
Anyone running SST is already running Pulumi's engine, regardless of whether they've written any Pulumi code.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails a platform team can enforce centrally, and components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used with the same engine SST already uses, without leaving it.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated, full-stack application framework, while Pulumi directly makes more sense when capabilities SST doesn't expose are needed (cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, infrastructure shared across applications).
Cross-references: the post links to /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
